data.title: Saudis shut down oil pipeline as Houthis tighten grip on Red Sea shipping
data.description:
Saudis shut down oil pipeline as Houthis tighten grip on Red Sea shipping

By Mohammed Ghobari, Eman Abouhassira and Yasmine Ghania
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 7:18 am UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Satellite image shows damage to the East-West pipeline facility in the Hejaz Region

1 of 7
Satellite image shows damage to the East-West pipeline facility in the Hejaz Region, Saudi Arabia, on September 11, 2026. 2026 Planet Labs PBC/Handout via REUTERS

By Mohammed Ghobari, Eman Abouhassira and Yasmine Ghania

ADEN/DUBAI, Sept 12 (Reuters) - Saudi Arabia has shut down its East-West pipeline after the vital oil conduit came under aerial attack in the widening Middle East war, threatening to send energy prices even higher.

The world's largest crude oil exporter temporarily closed the pipeline after a drone attack that both Baghdad and Riyadh said had originated in Iraq, ‌where Iranian-backed militias operate. Iraq dismissed a military commander on Saturday in response to the attack.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The 1,200-km (745-mile) pipeline running across the Arabian Peninsula had helped Saudi Arabia to bypass a shipping logjam in the ‌Strait of Hormuz, where tanker traffic has slowed to a trickle due to the six-month war between the U.S. and Iran.

The Saudi Energy Ministry said it had shut the pipeline as a precaution. The line has been moving 4 million to 5 million barrels per day in recent ​months, amounting to 4% to 5% of global supply, according to ship tracking companies and analysts.

It was not immediately clear who was responsible for the strikes. Satellite images showed black smoke rising from an area of the pipeline south of Medina. The attack resulted in some injuries and damage that was being assessed, the Saudi Foreign Ministry said without detailing the impact on exports.

The attack came as Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen tightened their grip in the Red Sea, which combined with the Strait of Hormuz disruptions has put an energy squeeze on both sides of the Arabian Peninsula and sent global oil prices back above $100 per barrel.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Four Yemeni government sources told Reuters that Houthis had seized the strategic island of Perim on ‌Friday at the mouth of the Red Sea, in the Bab el-Mandeb strait.

The ⁠dual attacks reported on Friday — on the pipeline and Perim Island — could represent a dangerous escalation while diplomatic efforts to end the war have stalled.

In a post on X on Saturday, Ebrahim Azizi, head of the Iranian parliament's national security committee, said: "As long as the American side does not accept all of Iran's conditions, dialogue and negotiation are of no use."

Saudi ⁠Arabia has asked Washington for military help with the Houthis, sources said, at a time when higher fuel prices during the war have already exacted a political toll on U.S. President Donald Trump and his Republican Party ahead of November congressional elections.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The East-West pipeline was hit on Thursday morning in Saudi Arabia's Riyadh and Medina regions, the Saudi Energy Ministry said.

The dismissed Iraqi military commander had led operations in Maysan province, according to Saturday's statement by the Iraqi prime minister's office. Maysan province, which borders Iran ​in ​southeastern Iraq, has long been regarded as an area where Iran-backed Shi'ite militias operate and maintain influence.

Saudi Arabia has opted against retaliation ​so far following a request from the Iraqi prime minister, the Saudi Foreign Ministry ‌said in a statement, though adding that the kingdom reserves the right to "take all measures necessary" to protect its interests. Iraq's government condemned the attacks.

Saudi crude supply fell to the lowest levels in more than three decades, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, partly due to attacks on ships transiting Bab el-Mandeb by Houthi-linked groups.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Iraq responded by ordering the closure of the Shalamcheh border crossing between Iraq and Iran as a precautionary measure, two security sources told Reuters. The crossing serves as one of the main routes for the import to Iraq of vegetables and other food supplies from Iran.

The two sources said a wide-scale operation was under way to find those responsible for the pipeline attack.

COUNTERATTACK PLANNED

If the Houthis gain control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait, their backer Iran could gain a critical advantage in its war with the U.S.

Yemeni government forces indicated they would try to retake areas captured by the Houthis — mountain fighters ‌who withstood years of devastating Saudi airstrikes during Yemen's civil war — in their lightning offensive this week along the Red Sea coastline.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Reuters ​reported on Thursday that the dramatic Houthi advance down Yemen's Red Sea coast came with direct guidance from Iran's Revolutionary Guards.

Iran told the ​Houthis last week to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia and promised more funding, weapons and senior ​officers to help them do so, two Iranian sources said.

Iran describes the Houthis as an ally but publicly denies giving them military direction, saying they are "not a proxy".

The Houthi military spokesperson, ‌Yahya Saree, said maritime navigation remained safe for all shipping except Saudi vessels subject ​to a previously announced ban.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

SAUDIS SEEK HELP

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed ​bin Salman called Trump at least twice on Thursday to request U.S. military help in fighting the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters on Friday, confirming an earlier report by Axios.

Washington told Riyadh it was not willing to take direct military action for now but would help with intelligence sharing and targeting, the two sources said.

The White House did not address a Reuters question on any phone calls ​between the two leaders, but a senior administration official speaking on the condition of ‌anonymity said Washington was in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Iran is expected to meet with Gulf states in Oman on Monday to discuss the Strait of Hormuz, the ​country's Foreign Ministry said on Friday.

(Reporting by Mohammed Ghobari in Aden, Eman Abouhassira and Maha El Dahan in Dubai, Yasmine Ghania, Menna AlaaElDin and Ahmed Tolba in Cairo, Catherine Cartier in Beirut, Samia ​Nakhoul in Ankara, and Jacob Bogage in Washington; Writing by Daniel Trotta; Editing by Kim Coghill and Tom Hogue)

data.title: Xi lands in India for BRICS summit overshadowed by war
data.description:
Xi lands in India for BRICS summit overshadowed by war

AFP News
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 6:59 am UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in New Delhi on Saturday for a BRICS summit alongside leaders from India, Russia and Iran as wars, trade and energy test the divided grouping.

The conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, along with global trade turbulence and energy security, will dominate the two-day meeting of the 11-nation bloc.

But Xi's visit is also being closely watched as his first to neighbouring India since 2019, and the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the nuclear-armed rivals.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Xi was given a red-carpet welcome, with an honour guard of soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses.

His arrival comes six years after a deadly 2020 military clash along their disputed Tibetan border, with ties gradually improving through restored flights, visas and high-level contacts.

Beijing said on Friday it was "ready to work with India... by strengthening communication, enhancing cooperation, and properly handling differences".

The underlying territorial dispute remains unresolved, and both sides retain heavy military deployments along their roughly 3,500-kilometre (2,175-mile) high-altitude border along Tibet.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

- 'Substantial harvest' -

Xi is due to hold face-to-face talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi later on Saturday, according to New Delhi's foreign ministry.

"They are looking for 'early and substantial harvest' when it comes to the border issue," said Pradeep Taneja, a China-India expert at the University of Melbourne.

"You cannot have a build-up of your forces on the border... but at the same time say 'we should continue to have people-to-people relations and economic relationships'."

Deep mistrust remains, with their contested Himalayan frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Dozens of Tibetans protested in New Delhi on Friday -- exiles, like their Buddhist leader the Dalai Lama, who has lived in India since fleeing a Chinese crackdown in 1959 -- waving placards against Xi's visit.

Modi embraced Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday before talks. Putin, who last visited India in December 2025, is one of New Delhi's most important strategic partners.

India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the US-Iran war in part by turning to Russia, despite Moscow's war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, also in New Delhi on Friday, said that pressure on Iran "has reached a critical and dangerous stage" following the "military aggression by the United States and Israel".

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Modi and Pezeshkian also held talks.

India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.

- 'Big constraint' -

BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.

Modi told leaders that BRICS nations "represent 50 percent of the world's population, 40 percent of global GDP, and more than 25 percent of global trade".

As well as Iran, BRICS includes Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates -- countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the United States and Israel in February.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi are also to attend.

Brazil is represented by Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira, with President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva campaigning for a fourth term in October elections.

BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.

"The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the BRICS summit," said Harsh V. Pant of India's Observer Research Foundation.

"What was seen until last year as an achievement -- the expansion of BRICS -- today looks like a big constraint on BRICS," Pant said.

data.title: Ukraine is fighting Russia anywhere it can – even in the deserts of Africa
data.description:
Ukraine is fighting Russia anywhere it can – even in the deserts of Africa

Ivana Kottasová, CNN
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 6:00 am UTC
10 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

The conditions are grueling. Temperatures regularly soar above 110 degrees Fahrenheit during the day, then drop sharply overnight. Water is scarce and the dust and sand get everywhere. But at least they are working above ground. This elite group of Ukrainian drone operators has spent years hunting Russians from dugouts in Ukraine. They are still doing the same – but in the desert in northern Mali.

Some 15 Ukrainian specialists have been deployed to the junta-led country in Africa's Sahel region to assist local rebel forces who are fighting Russian troops – part of Kyiv's mission to weaken its enemy wherever it operates. And Kyiv has also branched out to other theaters of conflict, capitalizing on its hard-won expertise in drone warfare to forge new anti-Russian partnerships.

Speaking to Ukrainian soldiers and officers involved in operations in Mali and Libya, CNN can reveal for the first time the extent of these operations on other continents. A Ukrainian Defense Intelligence source with knowledge of the operations told CNN that several Ukrainian specialists were also stationed in Sudan and that troops from Chad, Niger and Burkina Faso had previously traveled to Mali to receive drone training from Ukrainian soldiers there.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

When Iran began striking US allies in the Middle East earlier this year, Ukraine sent teams of military experts to at least five countries in the Middle East. They spent several weeks teaching local forces how to take down the Iranian-made Shahed drones which Russia has been using to terrorize Ukraine for several years. One Ukrainian soldier who was deployed to the United Arab Emirates told CNN they were operating in combined teams with local troops driving alongside them and mirroring their every move.

In exchange for sharing its know-how, Kyiv received an array of security cooperation agreements and promises of ammunition.

In the Sahel, a vast semi-arid region to the south of the Sahara Desert, the situation is more complicated.

Russia has been trying to assert itself as a power player in Africa, especially in the mineral-rich, coup-prone Sahel region. It has tried to fill the security void left by the withdrawal of French and other Western forces in recent years, propping up governments in exchange for cash and lucrative mining rights.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

At first, the Kremlin outsourced these operations to the Wagner Group, a private military company owned by entrepreneurial warlord Yevgeny Prigozhin. After Prigozhin's death following his attempted coup in 2023, Moscow merged what remained of Wagner with its regular military, creating the Africa Corps, which deploys in support of Moscow's local allies.

'Serious adaptation'

The Ukrainian group in Mali is embedded with a separatist group that calls itself the Azawad Liberation Front and is composed mostly of northern Tuareg rebels. They are not directly involved in the frontline fighting but provide the rebels with support, training and operational help, two Ukrainians deployed there told CNN.

"I coordinate their operations remotely. The signal from their drone comes to me over the internet, and I immediately tell them via radio what to do and where to fly," one of the Ukrainian drone operators currently in Mali told CNN.

"They go out on missions, then return to me, and we go over every detail of their actions. I don't go out to the front lines myself — that was a direct order from my superiors," he said.

Russia has previously accused Ukraine of participating in massacres against civilians in Mali – an accusation Kyiv has denied. Separately, rights group Human Rights Watch released two reports over the summer accusing Russian troops in Mali of killing civilians, and another report that said that "all parties" directly engaged in the conflict unlawfully attacked civilians during a flare-up in violence in April. The report did not mention Ukraine.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Asked about the allegations last month, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told reporters the Africa Corps "operates strictly within the bounds of legality" and "in response to official requests from the legitimate governments of African states."

The Ukrainian Defense Intelligence source told CNN the point of the overseas deployments is to put pressure on Russia and undermine the notion that Moscow can be a reliable ally. "We are turning our experience in the field of (drones) into a foreign policy tool," the source said.

But he said the mission is also beneficial to the Ukrainians because it gives them a chance to test their equipment and skills in a completely different environment – and to show partners their methods work everywhere.

"Dust and heat cause equipment to fail faster. Filters, cooling, electronics protection, batteries… everything works differently (and) requires serious adaptation," he said, adding that even the way the war is fought is vastly different.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"In Ukraine, it's high intensity, massive strikes, constant pressure. Here it's more of a maneuverable war over large territories, ambushes, route control, working in small groups and depending on knowledge of the terrain."

Differences in discipline and training require adaptation on both sides, he said, adding: "We teach them tactics; they teach us to survive and fight."

Russia is also using its operations in Africa to expand and adapt its military technology. Just this week, the state-owned weapons exporter, Rosoboronexport, presented new missiles and drones at the El Alamein International Airshow in Egypt, with the agency's chief telling the Russian state news agency TASS these weapons are "proven" for combat in Africa and the Middle East.

Growing confidence

The Ukrainian contingents are small, but they are a sign of Ukraine's growing confidence that its drone expertise has elevated its global status.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Héni Nsaibia, West Africa senior analyst at Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), an independent conflict monitor, told CNN that Mali is one of the countries where Russia now plays a crucial role.

"They provide an essential lifeline to the regime," he said, adding that Africa Corps forces have been "instrumental in preventing a more profound collapse, and possibly even the fall of the regime."

"But (the Russians) also need this military regime in place in order to be able to stay in Mali," Nsaibia added.

The first allegations that Ukraine was helping the Tuaregs came in 2024. In July that year, the rebels ambushed and killed dozens of Wagner fighters and Malian soldiers near the town of Tinzaouaten, on the border with Algeria.

Andriy Yusov, the spokesperson for Ukraine's Defense Intelligence, said at the time that the rebels received "necessary information" from Kyiv to fight the Russians. And while Ukraine later denied any substantial cooperation with the rebels, Yusov's comment prompted a backlash from the military juntas of Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso, who lodged an official complaint with the United Nations Security Council, accusing Ukraine of sponsoring terrorists.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

CNN asked Defense Intelligence for comment for this article and was referred to earlier comments made by officials.

The drone operator told CNN that Ukrainians also assisted rebels in the takeover of the strategic northern Mali town of Kidal earlier this year. The Tuareg rebels and militants linked to al Qaeda launched simultaneous attacks against the Russian troops, forcing them to withdraw. The Russian Defense Ministry accused Kyiv of playing a role in the attack, saying in a statement that "Ukrainian and European mercenary instructors" trained the rebels before the assault.

Nsaibia said the Kidal takeover marked a key defeat for the Malian regime – and the Russian troops that have been propping it up.

"It was a major setback that they lost Kidal and had to negotiate a safe corridor to be able to withdraw," he told CNN. However, Nsaibia said that the situation could have been much worse for the Malian regime, had it not been for the assistance of Russia's Africa Corps.

'Attacked by the same idiots'

The attack in Kidal highlighted the massive difference drones can make on the battlefield in Mali and elsewhere in the Sahel, where war still tends to be fought in more traditional ways, using infantry troops equipped with rudimentary weapons.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The Ukrainians in Mali told CNN the partnership with the Tuareg is one of convenience, not necessarily conviction.

"Culture and religion are different, but when you are being attacked by the same idiots, ideological differences fade into the background," the Defense Intelligence source said.

The drone operator told CNN that his personal opinions and feelings are irrelevant.

He described some of the rebels as "radicals" who are prone to spontaneously shoot in the air and act in "disruptive ways."

"Sometimes it's emotionally hard to ignore certain things. It just so happens that we're on the same side of the barricades right now… if these guys go on to successfully beat the Russians, we'll be more than happy to train them," he told CNN.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

He believes any operation that weakens the Russians can help Ukraine move the needle towards victory at home. "It puts pressure on them. This whole story has both psychological and real results," he told CNN.

A Russian 'shadow' fleet, and an escaped Ukrainian naval drone

Earlier this year, a group of Greek fishermen spotted a mysterious black vessel floating near the country's western island of Lefkada.

It turned out to be a Ukrainian naval drone carrying explosives. Greece issued a formal diplomatic protest to Ukraine and Kyiv officially apologized for the incident, but it blamed Russia for creating the situation by attacking Ukraine and using a "shadow" fleet of oil tankers. These allow Russia to sell its oil in defiance of international sanctions, helping to finance the war.

The drone had escaped from Ukrainian operators deployed to northwestern Libya, where they have been stationed since the end of 2025, the Ukrainian defense intelligence source told CNN.

Their presence there was first reported by French public broadcaster RFI in the spring, and while never officially confirmed by the Ukrainian government, it is now an open secret. One Ukrainian naval drone operator deployed in Libya told CNN his unit was using the international military base in Misrata as a launchpad to attack Russia's shadow fleet in exchange for training local forces.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Like the aerial drone operator in Mali, he was recruited earlier this year by Ukraine's Defense Intelligence straight from his previous post in Ukraine.

Ukraine – a longstanding contributor to UN-peacekeeping missions in northern and central Africa before Russia's full-scale invasion – has made no secret of its desire to become a different kind of player on the continent.

Kyrylo Budanov, Ukraine's former spy chief who is now the head of Zelensky's presidential office, said in 2023 that Ukraine's goal was to "keep killing Russians anywhere on the face of this world until the complete victory of Ukraine."

It's a sentiment shared by all the Ukrainian troops who spoke with CNN.

On Monday, Budanov once again pointed to Ukraine's growing global footprint, posting a statement on social media celebrating its Defense Intelligence for protecting the country's interests around the world, from "Russia to Africa, in a suit and in camouflage."

For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com

data.title: Syrian private airport plans spark outcry over mass graves, land rights
data.description:
Syrian private airport plans spark outcry over mass graves, land rights

By Feras Dalatey
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 5:06 am UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

FILE PHOTO: A view of the runway from the tower control room at military airport in the suburb of Mezzeh

1 of 7
FILE PHOTO: A view shows the runway from the tower control room at military airport in the suburb of Mezzeh where many Syrians died in detention, killed by execution, torture or maltreatment at the site that was widely feared, according to a report shared exclusively with Reuters by the Syria Justice and Accountability Centre tracing the deaths to seven suspected grave sites, on the outskirts of Damascus, Syria, January 12, 2025. REUTERS/Feras Dalatey/File Photo

By Feras Dalatey

DAMASCUS, Sept 12 (Reuters) - Syrian government plans to turn a former military airport in Damascus into a hub for private jets are raising alarm among rights groups and residents who say redevelopment could disturb suspected mass graves and override private land claims.

Syria's civil aviation authority said last week it was preparing to reclassify Mezzeh military airport ‌for limited civilian use, focused on private and executive aviation, to complement Damascus International Airport, according to a report on Syria's state news agency, SANA. Rubble removal and infrastructure upgrades had ‌already begun, the report said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The project is emerging as a test of how Syria's new authorities balance a drive to attract investment and redevelop state assets with two unresolved legacies of Assad's family rule: the fate of tens of thousands of missing Syrians ​and property rights clouded by decades of expropriation.

NEW DOCUMENTS SHOW AIRPORT'S ROLE AS EXECUTION SITE

Under ousted ruler Bashar al-Assad and his father Hafez, Mezzeh housed key branches of the powerful Air Force Intelligence Directorate, as well as numerous detention facilities where suspected government opponents were tortured, executed and subjected to enforced disappearance. Parts of the air base were used for presidential and other official flights.

Air Force Intelligence (AFI) documents recently obtained by the Syria Justice and Accountability Centre (SJAC), a U.S.-based Syrian-led human rights group, and shared exclusively with Reuters, show that senior Syrian military officials approved Mezzeh in 2012 as a site for carrying out executions of detainees sentenced to death by military ‌field courts.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

One document proposed moving executions from Sednaya — the country's most notorious prison ⁠at the time — to Mezzeh because it was a "closed security compound" close to Damascus. Subsequent correspondence discussed a firing range and later a hangar beside the runway as execution sites.

The documents, which underscore the central role of Mezzeh in the Assad-era security system, show officials ordered construction of a platform at the hangar, requested nylon rope and ⁠directed that the work be carried out under AFI supervision "in utmost secrecy."

A 2025 investigation by SJAC identified two suspected grave sites linked to people who died in detention at Mezzeh, where it said more than 1,150 detainees died, some by execution and others from torture or maltreatment.

In a July 2025 letter seen by Reuters, SJAC provided Syria's National Commission for Missing Persons with the coordinates of the two suspected graves inside the airport, urging authorities to prevent construction or excavation until ​the ​sites were investigated.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The commission told SJAC at the time that there were no construction or refurbishment plans for Mezzeh, ​SJAC told Reuters.

SJAC wrote to the commission again on September 8 after the redevelopment ‌plans emerged, warning that excavation, rubble removal or other works could damage human remains and evidence crucial to identifying victims, according to a second letter seen by Reuters.

SJAC told Reuters it had not yet received a response to its second letter.

Amer Matar, founder of the Syria Prisons Museum, a Germany-based NGO documenting detention facilities including those at Mezzeh, said the planned works showed a lack of respect for Syrian families who still have no answers on the fate of loved ones detained under Assad.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"To construct a business airport on a site that may contain mass graves, without a thorough prior investigation, without site protection, without searching for the missing and their remains, and without preserving evidence, is an act of extreme recklessness and disregard," Matar told Reuters.

The Syrian civil aviation authority, Syria's National Commission for Missing Persons and Syria's defense ministry, which ‌has been operating the airport, did not respond to questions from Reuters about suspected graves and land claims.

SANA cited the civil ​aviation authority's spokesperson as saying that Mezzeh's refurbishment would take into account the surrounding urban area and relevant legal and social issues, ​but did not specifically mention the graves or land rights. It is unclear who will develop ​the airport.

RESIDENTS PROTEST OVER LAND CLAIMS

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The dispute over the land on which airport facilities were built is decades old.

Under the Assads, private land was regularly expropriated for government ‌projects, often without compensation.

Mezzeh airport was built on land belonging to hundreds of ​private citizens across 2.76 sq km (1.1 square miles), according ​to land records from the Moadamiya municipality shared with Reuters.

A former municipal official, who asked not to be named, told Reuters that expropriation decrees retroactively justified the government's use of those lands when the airport was built in 1956, and that compensation had not been paid.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Residents demonstrated in Moadamiya a day after the redevelopment plans were announced. "We welcome investment, but we should be sitting at ​the table and discussing our share with investors, not the state," said one ‌protest organiser, who gave his name as Abu Khaled. "We have a documented right to this land."

The dispute comes as Syria faces calls to address Assad-era property seizures.

On September 2, ​United Nations land rights experts appealed to Syria's government to suspend and repeal laws they said had enabled systematic property dispossession under Assad, and to either establish mechanisms to ​return properties to their legitimate owners, or provide adequate compensation.

(Additional reporting by Maya Gebeily; Editing by Aidan Lewis)

data.title: Trump to visit Ireland's leaders before attending golf tournament
data.description:
Trump to visit Ireland's leaders before attending golf tournament

By Bo Erickson and Padraic Halpin
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 5:04 am UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

U.S. President Donald Trump visits Ireland

1 of 3
U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to members of the media before boarding Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, U.S. en route to Dublin, Ireland, September 11, 2026. REUTERS/Kylie Cooper

By Bo Erickson and Padraic Halpin

DUBLIN, Sept 12 (Reuters) - U.S. President Donald Trump will meet Ireland's leaders on Saturday before attending a golf tournament this weekend, a departure from his ‌recent focus on the Iran war and his party's effort to maintain power in November's midterm ‌elections.

The meetings with Ireland's president and prime minister are not part of an official state visit. But coming after this week's Republican ​convention and the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, the talks could include politically sensitive topics such as economic issues and Irish leaders' concerns over the Iran war.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump is making his 48-hour foreign trip as his Republican Party campaigns to keep its majorities in both chambers of the U.S. Congress. The Iran conflict has heightened economic concerns among ‌American voters by raising gas prices ⁠nationwide.

Anti-war and anti-Trump protests are planned in Dublin and in western Ireland near the Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg.

Ireland is one of the European Union's most pro-Palestinian ⁠countries and passed a law in July curbing goods trade with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. U.S. lawmakers and the American ambassador to Ireland criticized the law.

U.S., IRELAND TIES

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin has so far avoided political ​flaps with ​the U.S.

"The relationship between Ireland and the United States ​is very important economically," Martin told reporters when ‌asked about Trump's weekend trip. "It's very, very significant both ways."

U.S.-owned companies employ about 10% of workers in Ireland after successive governments prioritized their jobs and corporate tax revenue over decades, handing Ireland the healthiest public finances in Europe in recent years.

In Dublin on Saturday, Irish President Catherine Connolly, elected head of state last year, will have more direct interaction with Trump than she had during his first presidential visit in 2019. At the ‌time, Connolly, an outspoken politician with far-left views on foreign policy, ​protested Trump's visit outside Shannon Airport in western Ireland.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Now that Connolly ​is in the largely ceremonial role of president, ​some supporters have urged her to speak up against U.S. military actions around the ‌world and defend Ireland's neutrality.

Including Trump, eight sitting ​U.S. presidents have visited ​Ireland, starting with John F. Kennedy in 1963. But this trip has some hallmarks of Trump's typical weekends, which often revolve around golf outings at his company's properties.

The Trump Organization took control in ​2014 of the Doonbeg course, which ‌is hosting the Irish Open golf tournament this weekend. Trump is expected to help present the ​trophy on Sunday to the tournament champion.

(Reporting by Bo Erickson in Washington and Padraic Halpin ​in Dublin; Editing by Sergio Non and Rod Nickel)

data.title: ‘A f***-up of epic proportions’: Blame game begins after Iran-backed Houthis’ lightning advance down Red Sea coast
data.description:
‘A f***-up of epic proportions’: Blame game begins after Iran-backed Houthis’ lightning advance down Red Sea coast

Nic Robertson, Lauren Kent, CNN
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 4:00 am UTC
7 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

The desperate pleas for air cover from Yemeni generals started coming mid-morning on Thursday. An advance by the Iran-backed Houthis toward Yemen's strategic port city of Mocha was in full swing, and backup support from chief ally Saudi Arabia was nowhere in sight.

"The Houthis committed everything they had – waves upon waves of fighters … along with their available ballistic missiles and weapons," a senior Yemeni source attached to their military forces told CNN. The source said he contacted the United States Central Command (CENTCOM) and was assured the US was "watching the situation closely and that Saudi air support was coming."

"But the air support never came," the source said. "And Mocha has now fallen."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Hours later, on Friday, the Houthis captured another key coastal asset, Perim Island, at the mouth of the Red Sea. The island splits the Bab al-Mandeb Strait in two, giving Tehran de facto control over another key shipping route.

The Houthis' rapid advance amounts to an extraordinary 36 hours in a conflict that had been largely on ice for years. But the kindling for renewed fighting had been laid for months amid the conflict between the United States and Iran, as Tehran seeks to use oil prices – and their impact on the global economy – as leverage.

Now, Yemen and the Red Sea have the potential to become a true second front in the Iran war.

Iran's effective control of the Strait of Hormuz plus its tightening grip on the Bab al-Mandeb Strait threatens to push oil prices even higher, weeks before November's midterm elections in the United States.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

While the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the gateway to the Suez Canal shipping route, is less critical to global energy markets than Hormuz, it still carries essential goods worldwide, including millions of barrels of oil every day. The strait has become increasingly important since the start of the Iran war, as Saudi Arabia has re-routed some exports through the waterway to bypass Hormuz.

"(The Houthis) don't need to use advanced weapons to close Bab al-Mandeb. They can just use a cannon on a car," said Amr Al-Bidh, the top official of Yemen's Southern Transitional Council (STC). The STC has fought both the Houthis and Saudi-backed forces in the past, and wants an independent state in the south.

"It's a leverage that they have without using advanced weapons," Al-Bidh told CNN in an interview. "And they will keep it."

'Ghost' army rosters and no backup support

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke twice on Thursday with US President Donald Trump and urged him to strike the Houthis, another source familiar with the matter told CNN Friday. Trump declined to intervene, according to that source.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests—such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea—while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges," the White House said in response to CNN's questions about the calls. "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen Government regarding regional stability."

CNN has also reached out to the Saudi Embassy in Washington for comment.

The swift fall of Mocha and the lack of resistance have led to finger-pointing and recriminations among US allies.

"The failure this time is not with the Yemenis," a regional source told CNN on Thursday. "It's a disaster made in (Washington) DC and Riyadh.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The regional source told CNN that it was "a complete failure of political leadership" amid fierce squabbling and delayed decision-making in Riyadh.

"There was not one air strike throughout the day yesterday (by Saudi support forces), although there were minute-by-minute updates," the regional source added. "It's a Saudi-American f**k up of epic proportions."

Not everyone agrees. Mohammed al-Basha, who has served as an adviser to the US government and private sector on risks emerging from the Arabian Peninsula, argues that blame also rests with Yemeni leaders, whose internal divisions jeopardized their defenses.

"This goes back to a deeper problem in the anti-Houthi coalition," the DC-based told CNN. "There is no political cohesion."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"I think everybody was aware of the Houthis' push towards the west coast. The writings on the wall were very clear," he added. "There's no united command and control in Yemen."

Houthi fighters arrived in Mocha on Thursday to find Yemeni battalions that were severely depleted – their rosters were filled with "ghost names" receiving salaries, and the actual strength of the army was only about 20% of what it was on paper, a Western source with knowledge of the operations told CNN.

That was compounded by the fact that the United Arab Emirates – once a member of the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen – withdrew its remaining forces from the country in January, after Saudi Arabia called for them to leave amid a dispute. And Saudi Arabia did not backfill those troop barracks and bases.

"It doesn't make sense. I mean, you have the main backer of the militaries on the ground … who are really doing all of this work for 10 years, and suddenly you ask them to leave, and you don't fill that vacuum," Al-Bidh of Yemen's Southern Transitional Council added. "It's just lack of strategy and poor management."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The senior Yemeni official told CNN on Friday that he had "warned CENTCOM repeatedly over the past few days, including yesterday, that the situation was becoming critical." CNN has reached out to CENTCOM for response.

CENTCOM chief Adm. Brad Cooper was in Saudi Arabia on Thursday for coordination meetings, two sources familiar said. CENTCOM declined to comment, citing operational security reasons.

The Saudi military had been put on high alert three weeks ago, sources told CNN, but they didn't move key air command personnel into place. The Western source with knowledge of the battle said that Saudi Arabia never deployed the necessary service personnel to control and direct combat aircraft in the event of a serious attack.

"The Saudis threw the Yemenis under the bus," the Western source told CNN on Thursday.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

CNN has reached out to the Saudi Arabian information ministry for comment on those allegations.

The failure to defend Mocha and Perim is even more confounding in light of the recent news – reported exclusively by CNN – that more than 100 US military advisers were sent to Saudi Arabia providing intelligence and targeting support to the Kingdom in its military campaign, according to five sources familiar with the operations.

The US military personnel are working as part of a newly established joint forces command, which was formed in recent weeks amid signs Iran was ramping up its own efforts to aid Houthi attacks, said one of the sources, a US official. That official estimated the total number of US personnel in Saudia Arabia at roughly 200 troops.

The capture of the Red Sea assets gives the Houthis far greater maneuverability and leverage, as it opens up new locations from which the Iran-backed rebels can launch boats and attacks.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Asked what comes next, al-Basha, the risk analyst, told CNN: "I think the Houthis are going to be moving east. We are seeing today, via satellite and via OSINT (open-source intelligence) photography… that the Houthis are mobilizing."

An adviser to Iran's supreme leader on Friday described the Houthi advance on the west coast of Yemen as a "clear victory," writing in a post on X that "the American people and Washington's allies are paying the price for the economic crisis and Trump's ambitions."

CNN's Sarah El Sirgany, Mostafa Salem, Nadeen Ebrahim, Jennifer Hansler, Zachary Cohen, Katie Bo Lillis and Kylie Atwood contributed to this report.

data.title: Corruption probe targets Brazil presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro
data.description:
Corruption probe targets Brazil presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro

Facundo Fernández Barrio
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 4:23 am UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Revelations that Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering rocked his right-wing campaign Friday, weeks before elections.

Bolsonaro, the son of former leader Jair Bolsonaro, is vying for the presidency against leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in the October ballot.

A newly released court document revealed that police have been investigating Flavio Bolsonaro since July regarding possible crimes "in the context of financing the production" of a forthcoming film about his father.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Police conducted dozens of raids Thursday over the alleged embezzlement of public funds by the company that produced the flattering biopic.

"Dark Horse" -- starring US actor Jim Caviezel as Jair Bolsonaro -- has been under scrutiny as part of a widening corruption scandal that has loomed over the election.

"I have nothing to hide. The film is completely legal," Flavio Bolsonaro said at a campaign event on Friday.

An investigation of this kind does not prevent someone from running for office in Brazil.

Voters in Latin America's largest economy head to the polls on October 4, deeply polarized and with a weary sense of deja vu as Lula takes on Bolsonaro.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The 45-year-old senator Flavio Bolsonaro was thrust into the electoral race after his father was jailed for attempting a coup in 2022.

He has styled himself as a "more moderate" version of his firebrand father.

- Neck and neck -

The right-wing candidate has vowed to "rescue" Brazil from corruption, crime, high food prices and soaring public debt. His speeches are woven through with references to "God, country, family and freedom."

He has also pledged a heavy hand on crime, which polls show is voters' main concern.

While Lula has promised to prioritize the fight against organized crime, his challenger blames him for not taking violence seriously enough.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Bolsonaro's campaign has been hit by disclosures that he approached notorious fraud-accused banker Daniel Vorcaro -- head of the collapsed private bank Banco Master -- for money, which Bolsonaro said was to finance "Dark Horse."

According to court documents obtained by AFP, investigators believe Flavio Bolsonaro personally met with Vorcaro and discussed the film's financing with him on several occasions.

The documents also point to the transfer of $12.3 million from a company indirectly linked to Vorcaro to another tied to an attorney for Eduardo Bolsonaro, Flavio's younger brother.

A police source told AFP that the targets of Thursday's raids included Karina Gama, head of the company that produced "Dark Horse," and Mario Frias, a pro-Bolsonaro congressman listed as the film's executive producer.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Both have been banned from leaving Brazil pending the investigation's outcome. Frias has said he is innocent, denouncing the "smoke screen" probe.

Police officials said the money came from parliamentary funds available to lawmakers to finance special projects, usually in their electoral strongholds.

Vorcaro's alleged interactions with Supreme Court Judge Alexandre de Moraes, whom he apparently asked for legal help days before his arrest, have meanwhile triggered a crisis in Brazil's top court.

"The impact of corruption scandals is much greater for Lula's campaign than for Flavio's," said political scientist Mayra Goulart from the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

However, new evidence against Bolsonaro closer to the election could influence "voters whose choice is less clearly defined," she told AFP.

Lula was imprisoned for 580 days on corruption charges in 2018 and 2019, but his conviction was later overturned.

He and Flavio Bolsonaro are neck-and-neck in voting intentions ahead of the first round.

If, as expected, no one wins an outright majority, a runoff will be held on October 25.

data.title: Children in flood-hit Nepal grapple with loss, cling to hope
data.description:
Children in flood-hit Nepal grapple with loss, cling to hope

Paavan Mathema and Abhaya Srivastava
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 4:08 am UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

At 12, Nepali schoolgirl Ritu Maya Tamang has already learned how a close-knit family can be torn apart in a matter of minutes.

Tamang is among more than 500 children separated from their parents by the catastrophic August 26 flooding that hit the China-Nepal border, sweeping away homes, bridges and houses.

Nepal's disaster agency said Friday that 1,385 bodies had been retrieved, while 5,130 people remained missing. In China, state media says 43 people are dead and 519 missing.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The flood that first hit Nepal's high-altitude Rasuwa district claimed the life of Tamang's mother, but her body is yet to be found.

Tamang's younger sister is now battling pneumonia in hospital, and her father stays by her bedside.

While her life has been upended by the country's worst-ever flood disaster, one thing remains unchanged -- Tamang still wants to become a doctor.

"I get nightmares about the flood," the shy seventh grader said as she finished an essay in her neat handwriting at a temporary learning centre run by Save the Children charity in Nuwakot district. "But I have dreams."

Nearby, children -- some of them younger than five -- put finishing touches to colourful crayon drawings.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The memory of the day the floods struck is fresh in Tamang's mind.

Her mother, a housekeeper, was at work at a hydropower project office next to the Trishuli River.

"When the water came gushing, my mother could not escape it. I survived because I was at school," said Tamang, her eyes glistening with tears.

The only keepsake that Tamang has of her mother is a black face mask that she had tucked in her bag.

- Shock and trauma -

Save the Children says at least 540 children have been separated from their parents, and are living along with thousands others in relief camps in flood-affected areas, according to a preliminary assessment.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In one of the tented learning centres, teacher Shanti Sapkota said when the children first arrived, many were in a state of shock and panic.

"They would say that 'my house has been taken away', 'my father has been swept away' or 'my mother has been swept away'," Sapkota told AFP.

"But they are slowly moving on from that state of mind."

Nepal's government has said it will guarantee education through high school for affected children, with support ranging from residential care to full scholarships.

Along with its stakeholders, the government has committed to establishing a $6.5-million scholarship fund for some 1,000 students affected by the floods.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"We are giving priority to children who have lost their guardians," said education minister Sasmit Pokharel.

"We will identify what kind of support each child needs... We will stand by them," he said on Monday.

At the Nuwakot learning centre, psychologist Ekta Shreshtha said the children were easily triggered by any strange person or noise.

"It is still early days but from my observation, many of them are having trouble sleeping and have retreated into a shell," she told AFP.

"We try to keep them distracted with toys and other fun activities that help them forget their trauma for some time," she said.

"But their whole life is ahead of them. The pain is going to come back again."

data.title: Trump Floods Truth Social With Bizarre Posts On 9/11 Anniversary
data.description:
Trump Floods Truth Social With Bizarre Posts On 9/11 Anniversary

Anthony Orrico
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 3:48 am UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

While President Donald Trump spent much of the day delivering remarks during the Pentagon's 9/11 anniversary ceremony on Friday, he still found time for a bizarre mid-afternoon posting spree.

He posted about the crowd size at the Republican midterm convention, hype videos and a video from the January 6 insurrection, all while America marked the 25th anniversary of terrorist attacks that took the lives of nearly 3,000 people.

Trump kicked off the spree at 1:35 p.m. ET with a montage video from his Freedom 250 UFC fight on the White House lawn. 

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Just minutes later, he posted a video showing various news outlets announcing that he had won the 2024 presidential election.

Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost.

Trump followed that up at 2:51 p.m. ET, when he posted an infamous video from the Jan. 6, 2021 insurrection at the U.S. Capitol, where he told the rioters to "go home in peace."

Less than 30 minutes later, Trump maligned Democrats in a lengthy post for their criticism of his promised $5,000 dividend to every American adult if Republicans prevail in the midterms. 

"The $5,000 Trump Dividend, given to all Adults in the United States due to the fact that our Country is taking in Trillions of Dollars of Economic Development, Investment, and Pure SUCCESS, is being criticized by "Dumocrats" who are hoping that it never happens," Trump wrote. 

Trump then posted a video at 3:09 p.m. ET of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s speech at the Republican midterm convention. 

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

He capped off the posting bonanza just before 5 p.m. ET by sharing a series of articles boasting about the supposedly "sold-out" crowd at the convention, despite numerous videos from inside the event showing a bevy of empty seats.

Politics: Vance Heard Alarming Truth About Iran War In Secret Calls To Military Brass: NYT

Noticeably absent from Trump's posts was any mention of the 9/11 terrorist attacks. While Vice President JD Vance attended the annual remembrance ceremony in New York City on Friday, Trump was the only living president not in attendance. 

The New York Times reported in August that Trump was originally slated to attend the ceremony, but backed out in part because he wanted to deliver a speech, and organizers of the event have barred politicians from giving remarks since 2012 to maintain the solemnity of the ceremony.

data.title: Trump criticizes Smithsonian's focus on oppression
data.description:
Trump criticizes Smithsonian's focus on oppression

By Kanishka Singh
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 3:46 am UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Kanishka Singh

WASHINGTON, Sept 11 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump criticized what he called the Smithsonian's overwhelming focus on oppression on Friday and called for a five-year exhibition on George ‌Washington, in his latest critique of an institution he has repeatedly attacked.

The Republican leader ‌has denounced the Smithsonian for months, in what critics call part of a campaign to present U.S. history from a conservative ​point of view. On Tuesday, Smithsonian chief Lonnie Bunch said he was retiring.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump said on Truth Social that "under recently ended leadership," the Smithsonian took steps "to focus attention overwhelmingly on those who have been oppressed, but there is almost no attention paid to those who triumphed over great oppression, and against great odds."

"I am ‌calling on the Smithsonian Institution to ⁠honor the Life and Legacy of George Washington, America's Greatest Hero, with a five-year exhibition at the National Museum of American History, beginning now, and continuing ⁠through, February 22, 2032, the 300th anniversary of Washington's birth," Trump added.

Trump said he was also calling on the Smithsonian to "erect a 30-foot (9-m) 'Colossus statue'" of Washington outside the museum.

He also asked the Smithsonian to install an ​11-foot (3.4-m)statue of ​Washington that was featured at the recent Freedom 250 ​Grand Prix race in the museum's Flag ‌Hall.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The Trump administration has previously threatened to cut federal funding and federal agencies' support for the Smithsonian, with Trump expressing displeasure at what he called the institution's excessive focus on how bad slavery was.

Last year, his administration launched a review of some museums and his White House has accused the institution's National Museum of American History of "thinly veiled anti-Americanism."

Trump has also ordered installation of signs outside the museum ‌to reflect his administration's criticism.

Historians and civil rights advocates ​have denounced Trump's attacks and his accusations against the institution, ​saying such steps risk reversing social progress ​and undermine the acknowledgement of critical phases of U.S. history.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump says he aims ‌to remove "anti-American ideology."

Bunch has said the White House's ​accusations against the National ​Museum of American History were unfair.

The Smithsonian is a vast museum and research complex and a premier exhibition space for U.S. history and culture, with 21 museums and galleries and the ​National Zoo.

Trump has targeted U.S. cultural ‌and historical institutions - from museums to monuments to national parks - with his declarations and ​orders leading to the dismantling of slavery exhibits and the restoration of Confederate statues.

(Reporting ​by Kanishka Singh in Washington; Editing by Clarence Fernandez)
